Alkmaar, Holland. February 5, 1637.
A crowd is packed into a room behind an inn, and a man is holding up a sheet of paper.
On it is the name of a flower.
Not a flower anyone can see. It is a bulb, sitting in the dirt in a garden outside town.
The bidding starts. It climbs. And it keeps climbing.
When the hammer comes down, that one bulb has sold for more than five thousand guilders.

In the sixteen thirties, the Dutch Republic was the richest place on earth.
In the 1630s, the Dutch Republic was the richest place on earth.
Its ships traded spice from the East Indies, grain from the Baltic, and furs from the New World.
Amsterdam had the world's first real stock exchange. Its merchants were building tall new houses along the canals.
And for the first time, a lot of ordinary people had a little money to spare.
Weavers. Bakers. Innkeepers. Glassmakers.
People who wanted, more than anything, to look like they had made it.
The tulip was not Dutch.
It grew wild in the mountains of Central Asia, and the Ottoman sultans loved it. They planted it by the thousand in their palace gardens.
Even the name is Turkish. It comes from the word for a turban, for the shape of the flower.

He would not sell them. So people climbed his wall at night, and stole them.
Within a few years, tulips were growing all over Holland.
Most tulips were one color. Red, yellow, white.
But every so often, a plain tulip would bloom with flames of color running through the petals, like brush strokes.
The Dutch called them broken tulips. And there was no way to make one on purpose.
Nobody knew it then, but the flames were a disease. A virus, carried by tiny insects, that also made the bulb weak and slow to multiply.
So the most beautiful tulips were also the rarest, and the hardest to breed.
The most famous of all was called Semper Augustus. White, with flames of deep red.
In sixteen twenty three, a buyer offered twelve thousand guilders for ten of them.
In 1623, a buyer offered 12,000 guilders for ten of them.

Here is the strange part. A tulip blooms for about a week in spring.
The rest of the year, the bulb sits underground, where nobody can see it.
So by the winter of sixteen thirty six, people were not trading bulbs anymore.

They were trading promises. A slip of paper that said, I will sell you this bulb, at this price, when it comes out of the ground.
The deals were made in the back rooms of taverns, over wine.
Each tavern had its own rules. Groups called colleges met on set nights, and every deal paid a little wine money to the house.
The buyer often had no money yet. The seller often had no bulb yet.
The Dutch had a name for it. The wind trade.
And the prices went up.
A bulb bought in December could be sold in January for twice as much.
Then sold again, the same day, for more.
Even the plainest bulbs, the ones nobody had cared about a year before, went up more than ten times over in a few weeks.
That winter, a plague was also killing thousands of people in the town of Haarlem.
Some historians think that made people reckless. If you might not live till spring, why not take the bet?
It was no longer about the flower. Most of the buyers would never see the bulb they owned.
They only needed someone to buy the paper from them, for a little more than they paid.
A pamphlet from that winter lists what one rare bulb was worth, in things you could actually use.
Two loads of wheat. Four of rye. Four fat oxen. Eight fat pigs. Twelve fat sheep.

All of that... for one bulb, still in the ground.

And nobody bid.
Not at the price from last week. Not at half of it.
The news went from town to town in days. Everyone holding a promise to buy wanted out.
And everyone holding a promise to sell wanted to be paid.
Nobody has ever proved exactly why it stopped. Maybe the plague. Maybe the prices simply got too high for the next buyer.
The Alkmaar auction, with its five thousand guilder bulb, was one of the last good days.

Sellers took buyers to court. The courts did not want to know.
To the judges, these deals looked like gambling debts, and they would not enforce them.
In the end, towns worked out their own way out.

Preachers wrote pamphlets about the madness, and about God punishing greed.
One told of a sailor who ate a rare bulb, thinking it was an onion, and was thrown in jail.
Two hundred years later, a Scottish writer named Charles McKye put those stories in a best selling book.

It was called Extraordinary Popular Delusions and the Madness of Crowds. It has never gone out of print.
He said the whole country had gone mad. That the rich were ruined, and the crash was felt for years.
His book is where most of what we think we know about tulip mania comes from.
In the two thousands, a historian named Anne Goldgar went back to the Dutch archives. The court records, the contracts, the wills.
She could not find anyone who went bankrupt from tulips.
The traders were a few hundred people, mostly merchants and craftsmen. Not the whole country.
The Dutch economy did not stop. The richest years of the Golden Age were still ahead.
The bubble was real. The prices were real. The crash was real.
But the ruin... was mostly a story.
So why do we still talk about it?
Because it was the first time anyone wrote down the shape.
Something rare. Prices that only go up. People buying a promise, not the thing itself.
Buyers who don't care what it's worth, only what the next buyer will pay.

And then, one ordinary morning... the next buyer doesn't come.
Today, the Netherlands grows billions of tulip bulbs a year. You can buy one for less than a dollar.
The striped ones are bred now, not sick.
And the Semper Augustus, the flower nobody would sell, is gone. Not one is known to survive.
The question in that tavern was never, what is a tulip worth.
It was, who will buy it from me tomorrow.
